title: Routing and cascades as a cost lever
summary: A router picks a model per request, and a cascade tries a cheap model first and escalates when a check fails. Both save money only when query difficulty varies and quality is measured.
useIf: Most queries are easy, a few are hard, and you have an eval set that can tell them apart.
avoidIf: Tasks are uniformly hard, no eval set exists, or the prompt cache is your main saving.

explain.md: A **router** decides before the call which model should answer. A **cascade** calls a cheap model, checks the result and escalates only on failure. FrugalGPT reported a cascade that matched the best single model with up to 98% lower cost, or beat GPT-4 by 4% at equal cost, on 2023 benchmarks and prices [[r20]]. RouteLLM trained routers on preference data and cut cost by more than 2x in some settings with no quality loss [[r21]]. Treat these as proof the idea works, not as your savings.

Azure's **model router** is one deployment that routes per request across OpenAI, DeepSeek, Meta, xAI and Anthropic models. Modes are `Balanced` (the default, cheapest within about 1% to 2% of the best quality), `Cost` (about 5% to 6%) and `Quality`. Version `2025-11-18` is current and updates in place, while `2025-08-07` and `2025-05-19` are frozen. It runs on Global Standard and Data Zone Standard, reads text only, and its context window equals the smallest model in the pool [[r14]].

explain.title: Cascade break-even
explain.expr: cascade cost = c_cheap + c_check + p_escalate x c_strong; it wins when p_escalate < 1 - (c_cheap + c_check) / c_strong

vars.v: cost of one call on each model
cost of the verifier or validator
share of queries the check rejects

explain.example: c_strong = 10, c_cheap = 1, c_check = 0.5, p_escalate = 0.3: cost = 1.5 + 3 = 4.5, a 55% saving. Escalated queries also pay both latencies (derived).

explain.title: A cascade with a verifier
explain.alt: A query goes to a cheap model, a check accepts or rejects, rejected queries go to the strong model.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  Q[Query] --> C[Cheap model]
  C --> V{Check passes}
  V -->|yes| A[Answer]
  V -->|no| S[Strong model]
  S --> A

whereToUse: A support or search assistant with a wide spread of query difficulty
Extraction pipelines where a schema or rule check can verify a cheap model's output
One endpoint for many teams, using the Azure model router with a model subset
Classifying intent first, then sending only complex intents to the large model

use: A good share of traffic is easy and a smaller model passes your eval on it
A reliable verifier exists, such as schema validation, tests or retrieval overlap
Latency of an extra hop on hard queries is acceptable
avoid: The same model is cheap enough already and engineering time costs more
Quality evals do not cover the hard tail
Residency limits the pool so far that routing has little to choose from
flips: High escalation rate: cost approaches the strong model plus overhead, so use one model
Long shared prefix: routing across models splits the prompt cache, so measure both together
Context windows differ: the router uses the smallest model's window, so long prompts need a pinned subset

pitfalls.symptom: Quality dips with no deployment change
pitfalls.cause: The router version `2025-11-18` updates in place, so the model pool changed without a version bump [[r14]]
pitfalls.fix: Pin a model subset, keep a regression eval and a shadow comparison

pitfalls.symptom: Cache hit ratio fell after adding a router
pitfalls.cause: Consecutive requests reach different models, and each model has its own cache
pitfalls.fix: Measure cost with caching on both sides; use session affinity where offered, noting it is preview and no guarantee for Chat Completions

pitfalls.symptom: Escalations are common and cost went up
pitfalls.cause: The verifier is weak or the cheap model fails the hard tail
pitfalls.fix: Track escalation rate, tighten routing features, or drop the cascade

scenarios.title: A mixed-difficulty support assistant
scenarios.situation: An assistant handles thousands of questions a day. Most are simple look-ups, some need multi-step reasoning. A labelled eval set exists. Data may be processed globally.
constraints: An eval set with difficulty labels exists
unknowns: What share of queries is easy?
Does a long shared prefix make caching the bigger lever?
Who owns regressions after a router update?
scenarios.question: How do you cut cost without hurting quality?

options.name: Azure model router in Balanced mode with a pinned subset, shadow evals and rollback
options.why: One endpoint, per-request choice, and Balanced stays within about 1% to 2% of best quality by Microsoft's description.
options.tradeoff: Caching is split across models and the in-place version update needs monitoring.

options.name: Static rules by intent label
options.tradeoff: Rules go stale as models change and misroute hard queries.

options.name: Cascade where the cheap model grades its own answer
options.why: Self-grading is a weak verifier, so escalations or missed errors rise.
options.tradeoff: Right when a deterministic check exists, such as schema or tests.

flips.then: A single model with caching can beat routing.

flips.if: Prompts exceed the smallest pooled model's window
flips.then: Pin a subset of large-window models or route by length yourself.

scenarios.takeaway: Routing pays on wide difficulty spread with measured quality.

scenarios.title: Extraction with a hard validator
scenarios.situation: A pipeline extracts invoice fields. A schema check and a checksum validate every output. Volume is high and the cheap model is right about 85% of the time.
constraints: Failures can be retried on a stronger model
Batch is not possible, results feed a live form
unknowns: What does an escalation cost in latency?
Do validator failures correlate with document type?
scenarios.question: Which design fits?

options.name: Cascade: cheap model, validator, escalate failures
options.why: The verifier is reliable, escalation is about 15%, so cost is roughly c_cheap + 0.15 x c_strong.
options.tradeoff: The 15% of escalated requests pay two calls and two latencies.

options.name: Trained router on document features
options.why: Avoids paying twice on documents known to be hard.
options.tradeoff: Needs training data and misroutes unseen formats.

options.name: Always the strong model
options.why: It pays the large price for the 85% that are easy.
options.tradeoff: Right when the strong model is only slightly dearer or errors are unacceptable.

flips.if: Escalation rises above the break-even rate

flips.then: Do not cascade; use a router with evals or one model.

scenarios.takeaway: A cascade is only as good as its verifier.

quiz.q: A cascade has c_cheap = 1, c_check = 0.5 and c_strong = 10 (any unit). What is the highest escalation rate at which it still beats always using the strong model? Give the rate as a percentage.
quiz.explain: Break-even: 1.5 + p x 10 = 10, so p = 0.85. In practice latency and quality make the real threshold lower. Derived from the formula above.

quiz.q: After adding the Azure model router, prompt cache hits drop. Which cause fits best?
options: Consecutive requests reach different underlying models
quiz.explain: Caching helps only when consecutive requests reach the same model [[r14]]. The router does not rewrite prompts, and caching is not disabled but split.

quiz.q: Which changes favour a single pinned model over a router or cascade?
options: A long shared prefix dominates spend
Hard queries are rare and a verifier is reliable
There is no eval set that covers hard queries
quiz.explain: A dominant prefix, missing evals and a high escalation rate each remove the router's advantage. Rare hard queries with a reliable verifier favour a cascade.

flashcards.back: A router picks a model before the call. A cascade calls the cheap model first, checks the result and escalates on failure.

flashcards.front: What are the Azure model router modes?
flashcards.back: Balanced (default, within about 1% to 2% of best quality), Cost (about 5% to 6%) and Quality.
It splits the prompt cache across models, and the router's context window equals the smallest model in the pool.
